concepts: Rotation of a vector and projection of a vector
questions.question: The vector $\vec a=-\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ is rotated through a right angle, passing through the $y$-axis in its way, and the resulting vector is $\vec b$. Then the projection of $3\vec a+\sqrt2\,\vec b$ on $\vec c=5\hat i+4\hat j+3\hat k$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec b$ lies in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\hat j$, is perpendicular to $\vec a$, so $\vec b\parallel\vec a\times(\vec a\times\hat j)$.
solution: $\vec b$ lies in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\hat j$ and $\vec b\perp\vec a$, so $\vec b=\lambda\,\vec a\times(\vec a\times\hat j)$.
$\vec a\times(\vec a\times\hat j)=\vec a(\vec a\cdot\hat j)-\hat j|\vec a|^2=2\vec a-6\hat j=-2\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k$, so $\vec b=\lambda(-2\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k)$.
Rotation keeps the length: $|\vec b|=|\vec a|$, so $\sqrt6=\sqrt{12}\,|\lambda|$, giving $\lambda=\pm\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$.
$\lambda=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ is rejected because $\vec b$ must make an acute angle with the $y$-axis ($\vec b\cdot\hat j>0$ needs $\lambda<0$).
So $\lambda=-\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$ and $\vec b=-\sqrt2(-\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)=\sqrt2\hat i+\sqrt2\hat j-\sqrt2\hat k$.
Projection on $\vec c$ $=\dfrac{(3\vec a+\sqrt2\vec b)\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}=\dfrac{-5+32+3}{\sqrt{50}}=\dfrac{30}{5\sqrt2}=3\sqrt2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $\vec b=\lambda\vec a\times(\vec a\times\hat j)\Rightarrow\vec b=\lambda(-2\hat i-2\hat j+2\hat k)\vec a$ (a stray $\vec a$ at the end); the expansion of the triple product, the check $\vec b\cdot\hat j>0$ and the final dot product were not shown and are added. Result $3\sqrt2$ unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Build $\vec b$ directly as the unit direction of the component of $\hat j$ perpendicular to $\vec a$, scaled to $|\vec a|$; then project term by term.
solution: The component of $\hat j$ perpendicular to $\vec a$ is $\hat j-\dfrac{\hat j\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a=\hat j-\dfrac{\vec a}{3}=\left(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,-\tfrac13\right)$.
Rotating $\vec a$ through $90^\circ$ towards (and past) $\hat j$ gives $\vec b$ along this direction, so $\vec b=\sqrt6\cdot\dfrac{(1,1,-1)}{\sqrt3}=\sqrt2(1,1,-1)$.
Projection is linear: $\vec a\cdot\vec c=-5+8+3=6$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\sqrt2(5+4-3)=6\sqrt2$.

useful_results: For any vectors $\vec a,\vec u$: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec u)=\vec a(\vec a\cdot\vec u)-\vec u|\vec a|^2$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$, lies in their plane and points away from $\vec u$.

A $90^\circ$ rotation of $\vec a$ within the plane of $\vec a,\vec u$ towards $\vec u$ gives $|\vec a|\,\dfrac{\vec u_\perp}{|\vec u_\perp|}$, where $\vec u_\perp=\vec u-\dfrac{\vec u\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a$.
The scalar projection of $\vec x$ on $\vec c$ is $\dfrac{\vec x\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}$; it is linear in $\vec x$, so project each term separately.

concepts: Projection of a vector
Cosine rule in a triangle
questions.question: In a triangle $ABC$, if $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=8,\ |\overrightarrow{CA}|=7,\ |\overrightarrow{AB}|=10$, then the projection of the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is $|AB|\cos A$, and $\cos A$ comes from the cosine rule.
solution: Let $\theta=\angle A$ be the angle between $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$; projection $=|\overrightarrow{AB}|\cos\theta=10\cos\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $A$ at the origin and $C$ on the $x$-axis; the projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is just the $x$-coordinate of $B$.
solution: The projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ (which lies along the $x$-axis) is $x=\dfrac{85}{14}$.

useful_results: In $\triangle ABC$ with sides $a,b,c$, the projection of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ on $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is $c\cos A=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2b}$ (here $\dfrac{49+100-64}{14}=\dfrac{85}{14}$).
Equivalently $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2}$ (polarisation of $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=|\overrightarrow{AC}-\overrightarrow{AB}|^2$).
Projections of the sides on one another satisfy $a=b\cos C+c\cos B$ (projection formula).

concepts: Equation of a plane in intercept form
Algebraic identity for $a+b+c=0$
questions.question: If $(x,y,z)$ is an arbitrary point on the plane $P$ passing through $(42,0,0),(0,42,0),(0,0,42)$, then $3+\dfrac{x-11}{(y-19)^2(z-12)^2}+\dfrac{y-19}{(x-11)^2(z-12)^2}+\dfrac{z-12}{(x-11)^2(y-19)^2}-\dfrac{x+y+z}{14(x-11)(y-19)(z-12)}$ is equal to:
solution: The expression becomes $3+\dfrac a{b^2c^2}+\dfrac b{a^2c^2}+\dfrac c{a^2b^2}-\dfrac{42}{14abc}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The value is the same for every point of the plane, so evaluate at one convenient point.
solution: The answer is constant on the plane, so choose $a=1,\ b=1,\ c=-2$ (i.e. $(x,y,z)=(12,20,10)$, and $12+20+10=42$ is on the plane).
$\dfrac a{b^2c^2}=\dfrac14,\ \dfrac b{a^2c^2}=\dfrac14,\ \dfrac c{a^2b^2}=-2$, which add up to $-\dfrac32$.

useful_results: If $a+b+c=0$ then $a^3+b^3+c^3=3abc$ (from $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca)$).
The plane through $(p,0,0),(0,p,0),(0,0,p)$ is $x+y+z=p$.
When a question says the value is the same for 'an arbitrary point' of a plane or line, test one convenient point to find (or check) the answer.

concepts: Coplanar vectors and angle bisector of two vectors
questions.question: A vector $\vec a=\alpha\hat i+2\hat j+\beta\hat k\ (\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R)$ lies in the plane of the vectors $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$ and $\vec c=\hat i-\hat j+4\hat k$. If $\vec a$ bisects the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, then:
questions.key_idea: A vector along a bisector of $\vec b,\vec c$ is $\hat b\pm\hat c$; only the external one ($\hat b-\hat c$) matches an option.
solution: $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar: $\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&2&\beta\\1&1&0\\1&-1&4\end{vmatrix}=0$, i.e. $4\alpha-8-2\beta=0$ (this relation is checked below).
If $\vec a$ is along the bisector, $\vec a=\lambda(\hat b+\hat c)=\lambda\left(\dfrac{\hat i+\hat j}{\sqrt2}+\dfrac{\hat i-\hat j+4\hat k}{3\sqrt2}\right)$.
So $\alpha\hat i+2\hat j+\beta\hat k=\lambda\left(\dfrac4{3\sqrt2}\hat i+\dfrac2{3\sqrt2}\hat j+\dfrac4{3\sqrt2}\hat k\right)$.
Then $\alpha=4,\ \beta=4$, $\vec a=4\hat i+2\hat j+4\hat k$, which satisfies none of the options.
So take the other bisector (of the pair $\vec b,-\vec c$): $\vec a=\mu(\hat b-\hat c)=\mu\left(\dfrac2{3\sqrt2}\hat i+\dfrac4{3\sqrt2}\hat j-\dfrac4{3\sqrt2}\hat k\right)$.
Comparing the $\hat j$ term: $\dfrac{4\mu}{3\sqrt2}=2\Rightarrow\mu=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}2$, giving $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$.
Hence $\vec a\cdot\hat k=-2$, i.e. $\vec a\cdot\hat k+2=0$.
questions.correction_note: Two points. (1) The PDF's coplanarity determinant has the middle entry $1$ in the first row; it should be $2$ (the $\hat j$ coefficient of $\vec a$): $4\alpha-8-2\beta=0$. Both $(4,2,4)$ and $(1,2,-2)$ satisfy the corrected relation. (2) Strictly, the internal bisector of the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $\vec a=(4,2,4)$, which matches no option; the key (B) is the vector along $\hat b-\hat c$ (external bisector). The key (B) is kept because it is the only option consistent with the problem, but the stem is loosely worded.

alternate_solutions.idea: A vector on a bisector makes equal angles with $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, so $\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}=\pm\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}$; combine each sign with coplanarity.
solution: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\alpha+2$, $|\vec b|=\sqrt2$; $\vec a\cdot\vec c=\alpha-2+4\beta$, $|\vec c|=3\sqrt2$.
Sign $+$: $3(\alpha+2)=\alpha-2+4\beta\Rightarrow\beta=\dfrac{\alpha+4}2$; with $\beta=2\alpha-4$ this gives $\alpha=4,\ \beta=4$ (no option matches).
So $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$ and $\vec a\cdot\hat k+2=0$, option (B).

useful_results: Vectors along the two bisectors (internal and external) of the angle between $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are $\hat b+\hat c$ and $\hat b-\hat c$.
$\vec a$ lies in the plane of $\vec b,\vec c$ iff $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$.

A vector $\vec a$ in the plane makes equal angles with $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ iff $\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}$ (internal bisector line); with a minus sign it is the external one.
When an answer is to be matched with options and the first natural case fails to match, check the other bisector (the sign ambiguity).

concepts: Position vectors of triangle centres (Euler line)
questions.question: If the points $P$ and $Q$ are respectively the circumcentre and the orthocentre of a $\triangle ABC$, then $\overrightarrow{PA}+\overrightarrow{PB}+\overrightarrow{PC}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The centroid $G$ lies on $PQ$ with $PG:GQ=1:2$, so $3\overrightarrow{PG}=\overrightarrow{PQ}$.
solution: Take position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ of $A,B,C$ with the circumcentre $P$ as the origin.
The centroid $G$ has $\overrightarrow{PG}=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b+\vec c}3$.
$G$ divides $PQ$ (circumcentre to orthocentre) in the ratio $1:2$, so $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=3\overrightarrow{PG}=\overrightarrow{PQ}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test a right triangle, where the orthocentre is the right-angle vertex and the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

useful_results: With the circumcentre as origin, the orthocentre is $H=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$ and the centroid is $G=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b+\vec c}3$ (Sylvester's relation); $O,G,H$ are collinear with $OG:GH=1:2$.
For a right triangle the orthocentre is the right-angle vertex and the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse - a quick test case.
If the circumcentre is $O$ then $\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{OH}$.

concepts: Vector triple product and scalar product of two cross products
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be non-zero vectors with $\vec b\cdot\vec c=0$ and $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=\dfrac{\vec b-\vec c}2$. If $\vec d$ is a vector with $\vec b\cdot\vec d=\vec a\cdot\vec b$, then $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Expand the triple product to read off $\vec a\cdot\vec c$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b$, then use $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec d)-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$.
solution: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c=\dfrac{\vec b}2-\dfrac{\vec c}2$.
$\vec b,\vec c$ are non-zero and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=0$, so they are not parallel; comparing coefficients, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=\dfrac12$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\dfrac12$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec d)-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose coordinates adapted to the data ($\vec b\perp\vec c$) and compute both cross products explicitly.
solution: Take $\vec b=\hat i,\ \vec c=\hat j$ (then $\vec b\cdot\vec c=0$ and $\vec b\times\vec c=\hat k$).
$\vec a\times\hat k=(a_y,-a_x,0)$ must equal $\dfrac{\vec b-\vec c}2=\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,0\right)$, so $\vec a=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,t\right)$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec d=\vec a\cdot\vec b=\tfrac12$ gives $\vec d=\left(\tfrac12,d_y,d_z\right)$.

useful_results: BAC-CAB: $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.
Lagrange/Binet-Cauchy identity: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec d)-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$.
If $\vec b,\vec c$ are non-parallel and $x\vec b+y\vec c=\vec 0$ then $x=y=0$; this lets you compare coefficients in a vector equation.

concepts: Line parallel to a plane and intersecting a given line
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the line $L$ pass through $(0,1,2)$, intersect the line $\dfrac{x-1}2=\dfrac{y-2}3=\dfrac{z-3}4$ and be parallel to the plane $2x+y-3z=4$. Then the distance of $P(1,-9,2)$ from $L$ is:
questions.key_idea: $L$ joins $A(0,1,2)$ to a point $B$ of the given line, and $\overrightarrow{AB}\perp$ normal of the plane fixes $B$.
solution: Let $A=(0,1,2)$ and let $L$ meet the given line at $B(1+2\lambda,\,2+3\lambda,\,3+4\lambda)$.
$L$ is parallel to the plane, so $\overrightarrow{AB}\perp\vec n=(2,1,-3)$: $(1+2\lambda,1+3\lambda,1+4\lambda)\cdot(2,1,-3)=0$.
So $B=(1,2,3)$ and $L:\ \vec r=\hat j+2\hat k+\mu(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)$.
Let $Q(\mu,\,1+\mu,\,2+\mu)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P(1,-9,2)$; $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(\mu-1,\,10+\mu,\,\mu)$.
questions.correction_note: Minor sign slip: the PDF writes $5\lambda=0$; the expansion $2+4\lambda+1+3\lambda-3-12\lambda$ equals $-5\lambda$. $\lambda=0$ and the answer $\sqrt{74}$ are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the cross-product distance formula $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$, with no foot of perpendicular.
solution: Direction of $L$ is $\vec d=(1,1,1)$ (as found from $\lambda=0$) and $A=(0,1,2)$ is on $L$.
Distance$^2=\dfrac{222}{|\vec d|^2}=\dfrac{222}3=74$, so the distance is $\sqrt{74}$.

useful_results: Distance of a point $P$ from the line through $A$ with direction $\vec d$ is $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ (here $\sqrt{74}$).
A line with direction $\vec d$ is parallel to the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ iff $\vec d\cdot\vec n=0$.
To find a line through a point $A$ meeting a given line: write the general point $B$ of that line and impose the extra condition (here $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vec n=0$) on $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

concepts: Cross product orthogonality and dot product of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec u=\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k,\ \vec v=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k,\ \vec v\cdot\vec w=2$ and $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u+\lambda\vec v$. Then $\vec u\cdot\vec w$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec v\times\vec w$ is perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec w$, so dotting the given equation with $\vec v$ and then $\vec w$ removes the cross product.
solution: Dot with $\vec v$: $(\vec v\times\vec w)\cdot\vec v=\vec u\cdot\vec v+\lambda\vec v\cdot\vec v\Rightarrow0=\vec u\cdot\vec v+\lambda|\vec v|^2$.
Dot with $\vec w$: $(\vec v\times\vec w)\cdot\vec w=\vec u\cdot\vec w+\lambda\vec v\cdot\vec w\Rightarrow0=\vec u\cdot\vec w+2\lambda$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $(\vec v\times\vec w)\vec v=\ldots$ and $(\vec v\times\vec w)\vec w=\ldots$ without the dot between the factors; the dot product is meant. Values and answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\vec w$ itself: from $\vec v\times(\vec v\times\vec w)=\vec v(\vec v\cdot\vec w)-\vec w|\vec v|^2$.
solution: With $\lambda=-\tfrac12$, $\vec s=\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u-\tfrac12\vec v=\left(0,-\tfrac32,-\tfrac32\right)$.
$\vec v\times\vec s=\vec v(\vec v\cdot\vec w)-\vec w|\vec v|^2=2\vec v-6\vec w$.
$\vec v\times\vec s=(2,1,-1)\times\left(0,-\tfrac32,-\tfrac32\right)=(-3,3,-3)$, so $6\vec w=2\vec v-(-3,3,-3)=(7,-1,1)$ and $\vec w=\tfrac16(7,-1,1)$.
Check: $\vec v\cdot\vec w=\dfrac{14-1-1}6=2$ and $\vec u\cdot\vec w=\dfrac{7+1-2}6=1$.

useful_results: $\vec v\times\vec w$ is perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec w$, so $(\vec v\times\vec w)\cdot\vec v=(\vec v\times\vec w)\cdot\vec w=0$.
Whenever an equation has the form $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec p$, dotting with $\vec v$ or $\vec w$ kills the left side and gives scalar equations.
$\vec v\times(\vec v\times\vec w)=\vec v(\vec v\cdot\vec w)-\vec w|\vec v|^2$ recovers $\vec w$ from $\vec v\times\vec w$ and $\vec v\cdot\vec w$.

concepts: Section formula, equation of a plane and distance in 3D
questions.question: The plane $2x-y+z=4$ intersects the line segment joining $A(a,-2,4)$ and $B(2,b,-3)$ at the point $C$ in the ratio $2:1$ and the distance of $C$ from the origin is $\sqrt5$. If $ab<0$ and $P$ is the point $(a-b,\,b,\,2b-a)$, then $CP^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Section formula gives $C$ in terms of $a,b$; the plane gives $a-b=2$ and $OC=\sqrt5$ gives a quadratic in $b$, solved with $ab<0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $C$ first as a point of the plane lying on the sphere $|OC|^2=5$ with $z=-\tfrac23$, then recover $a,b$ from the section formula.
solution: From $x=\dfrac{a+4}3,\ y=\dfrac{2b-2}3$: $(x,y)=\left(\tfrac53,-\tfrac43\right)$ gives $(a,b)=(1,-1)$, while $\left(\tfrac{31}{15},-\tfrac8{15}\right)$ gives $\left(\tfrac{11}5,\tfrac15\right)$ with $ab>0$ (rejected).

useful_results: A point dividing $AB$ internally in the ratio $m:n$ is $\dfrac{n\vec A+m\vec B}{m+n}$; for any linear $f=px+qy+rz-s$, $f(C)=\dfrac{n f(A)+m f(B)}{m+n}$, so $f(C)=0$ gives $n f(A)+m f(B)=0$ at once.
Here $f(A)=2a+2$, $f(B)=-b-3$, and $f(A)+2f(B)=0$ gives $a-b=2$.
Squared-distance conditions give quadratics; use any sign condition ($ab<0$) to discard roots.

concepts: Rotation of axes and components of a vector
questions.question: A vector $\vec a$ has components $3p$ and $1$ with respect to a rectangular cartesian system. The system is rotated through a certain angle about the origin in the counter-clockwise sense. If, with respect to the new system, $\vec a$ has components $p+1$ and $\sqrt{10}$, then a value of $p$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A rotation of the axes does not change the length of the vector.
solution: The length of $\vec a$ does not change under rotation of axes: $\sqrt{(3p)^2+1^2}=\sqrt{(p+1)^2+(\sqrt{10})^2}$.
$p=-1$ or $p=\dfrac54$; the only value among the options is $p=-1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the four options directly against the invariance $x^2+y^2=x'^2+y'^2$.
solution: $p=-1$: $9+1=10$ and $0+10=10$; equal lengths, so a rotation exists (components $(-3,1)\to(0,\sqrt{10})$).

useful_results: Under rotation of axes the components $(x,y)\to(x',y')$ satisfy $x^2+y^2=x'^2+y'^2$; the transformation $x'=x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta,\ y'=-x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta$ is length-preserving.
Two quantities that must be equal under a transformation give an equation in the unknown directly; the angle itself is never needed.
A quadratic can give two roots ($p=-1,\ \tfrac54$); pick the one listed among the options.

concepts: Angle between two vectors
Sum of cosines of angles in arithmetic progression
questions.question: Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ with $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$. If $a\cos\theta=b\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{2\pi}3\right)=c\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{4\pi}3\right)$, where $\theta=\dfrac\pi9$, then the angle between the vectors $a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ and $b\hat i+c\hat j+a\hat k$ is:
questions.key_idea: Equal products give $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c\propto\cos\theta+\cos\left(\theta+\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)+\cos\left(\theta+\tfrac{4\pi}3\right)=0$, so $ab+bc+ca=0$.
solution: $K\neq0$: otherwise $a=b=c=0$ (none of the three cosines is zero for $\theta=\tfrac\pi9$), contradicting $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF divides by $a,b,c$ and uses $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c$ without checking that $K\neq0$ and $abc\neq0$; this justification is added (otherwise $a=b=c=0$, contradicting $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$). Result unchanged.
useful_results: For any $\theta$: $\cos\theta+\cos\left(\theta+\tfrac{2\pi}3\right)+\cos\left(\theta+\tfrac{4\pi}3\right)=0$ (three equally spaced unit phasors add to zero); same for sines.
If $ax=by=cz=K\neq0$ then $a,b,c\propto\dfrac1x,\dfrac1y,\dfrac1z$; so $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac1c=\dfrac{x+y+z}K$.
The angle between $(a,b,c)$ and its cyclic shift $(b,c,a)$ has $\cos=\dfrac{ab+bc+ca}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$; it is $\dfrac\pi2$ iff $ab+bc+ca=0$.
Always rule out $K=0$ (the degenerate case) before dividing.

concepts: Vector triple product and cross product of vectors
questions.question: Let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $\vec a=\lambda\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k,\ \vec b=\hat i-\lambda\hat j+2\hat k$. If $\big((\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\big)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=8\hat i-40\hat j-24\hat k$, then $\big|\lambda(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)\big|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Use $\vec X\times(\vec a-\vec b)=(\vec b-\vec a)\times\vec X$ and BAC-CAB: the expression collapses to $(|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2)(\vec a\times\vec b)$.
solution: $\big((\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\big)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=(\vec b-\vec a)\times\big((\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\big)$.
BAC-CAB: $=(\vec a+\vec b)\big((\vec b-\vec a)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)\big)-(\vec a\times\vec b)\big((\vec b-\vec a)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)\big)$; the first bracket is $0$.
So the expression $=(|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2)(\vec a\times\vec b)$, with $|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2=(\lambda^2+13)-(\lambda^2+5)=8$.
Thus $8(\vec a\times\vec b)=8\hat i-40\hat j-24\hat k$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\lambda&2&-3\\1&-\lambda&2\end{vmatrix}=(4-3\lambda)\hat i-(2\lambda+3)\hat j+(-\lambda^2-2)\hat k$.
$\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k,\ \vec b=\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$, so $\vec a+\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec a-\vec b=3\hat j-5\hat k$.
$(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&1&-1\\0&3&-5\end{vmatrix}=-2\hat i+10\hat j+6\hat k$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=2\hat i+10\hat j+6\hat k$; the $\hat i$ coefficient is $1\cdot(-5)-(-1)(3)=-2$, so the vector is $-2\hat i+10\hat j+6\hat k$ (equal to $-2\,\vec a\times\vec b$). The squared length $4+100+36=140$ and the answer are unchanged. The PDF also jumps from the triple product to $8(\vec a\times\vec b)$; the BAC-CAB step is added.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so the given vector (a multiple of $\vec a\times\vec b$) must be perpendicular to $\vec a$; this gives $\lambda$ at once. Also $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-2\,\vec a\times\vec b$.
solution: As in the main solution, the given vector equals $8(\vec a\times\vec b)$, so $\vec a\times\vec b=(1,-5,-3)$.
This is perpendicular to $\vec a=(\lambda,2,-3)$: $\lambda-10+9=0\Rightarrow\lambda=1$ (no cross product needs to be expanded).
$(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec a=-2(\vec a\times\vec b)=(-2,10,6)$.

useful_results: $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-2\,\vec a\times\vec b$.
$\big((\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\big)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=(|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2)(\vec a\times\vec b)$ for all $\vec a,\vec b$ (verified here with $\lambda=1$: $8(1,-5,-3)$).
$\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to both $\vec a$ and $\vec b$: a vector known to be a multiple of $\vec a\times\vec b$ gives scalar equations by dotting with $\vec a$ or $\vec b$.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ (Lagrange).

concepts: Plane through the intersection of two planes
Perpendicular planes
questions.question: If the plane containing the line $x+2y+3z-4=0=2x+y-z+5$ and perpendicular to the plane $\vec r=(\hat i-\hat j)+\lambda(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)+\mu(\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k)$ is $ax+by+cz=4$, then $a-b+c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A plane through the line is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; its normal must be perpendicular to the normal $(1,1,1)\times(1,-2,3)$ of the given plane.
solution: A plane containing the line of intersection of the two planes: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0\Rightarrow(1+2\lambda)x+(2+\lambda)y+(3-\lambda)z+(5\lambda-4)=0$ ....(1)
The given plane $\vec r=(\hat i-\hat j)+\lambda(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)+\mu(\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k)$ ....(2)
Normal of plane (2) $=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&1&1\\1&-2&3\end{vmatrix}=5\hat i-2\hat j-3\hat k$.
Planes (1) and (2) are perpendicular, so their normals are perpendicular: $5(1+2\lambda)-2(2+\lambda)-3(3-\lambda)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the plane's normal as a cross product: it is perpendicular to the line's direction and to the given plane's normal.
solution: The required normal $\vec n$ is perpendicular to this direction and to $(5,-2,-3)$ (the normal of the given plane): $\vec n\parallel(-5,7,-3)\times(5,-2,-3)=(-27,-30,-25)$.
So the plane is $27x+30y+25z=k$. The line passes through $(-\tfrac{14}3,\tfrac{13}3,0)$ (put $z=0$ in both planes).

useful_results: Every plane through the line $P_1=0=P_2$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (one parameter).
Planes are perpendicular iff their normals are perpendicular ($\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2=0$).
The plane $\vec r=\vec r_0+\lambda\vec u+\mu\vec v$ has normal $\vec u\times\vec v$.
A plane containing a line and perpendicular to a plane has normal $=\vec d\times\vec n_2$.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular on a plane and distance between points
questions.question: If for $a>0$ the feet of the perpendiculars from $A(a,-2a,3)$ and $B(0,4,5)$ on the plane $lx+my+nz=0$ are $C(0,-a,-1)$ and $D$ respectively, then the length of segment $CD$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\overrightarrow{CA}$ is normal to the plane and $C$ lies on it; this fixes $a$, then $D$ is the foot from $B$ along the normal.
solution: The normal of the plane is along $\overrightarrow{CA}=(a-0,\,-2a+a,\,3+1)=(a,-a,4)$.
The plane passes through the origin: $ax-ay+4z=0$.
Line $BD$ (through $B$ along the normal): $\vec r=(0,4,5)+\lambda(1,-1,2)$, so $D(\lambda,\,4-\lambda,\,5+2\lambda)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the normal as $\overrightarrow{AC}=(a,-a,-4)$ but then uses $ax-ay+4z=0$; the normal along $\overrightarrow{CA}$ is $(a,-a,4)$ (with $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-a,a,-4)$). The plane $x-y+2z=0$, $a=2$, $D$ and the answer are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $CD$ is the projection of $AB$ on the plane, so $CD^2=AB^2-(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\hat n)^2$.
solution: As before $\vec n\parallel(a,-a,4)$ and $a=2$, so $\hat n=\dfrac{(1,-1,2)}{\sqrt6}$.

useful_results: For a plane through the origin and the foot $C$ of the perpendicular from $A$: the normal is along $\overrightarrow{CA}$ and $\vec n\cdot\vec C=0$.
If $C,D$ are the feet of perpendiculars from $A,B$ on a plane with unit normal $\hat n$, then $CD^2=AB^2-(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\hat n)^2$ (here $72-6=66$).
Foot of the perpendicular from $B$ on $ax+by+cz+d=0$: $B-\dfrac{ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d}{a^2+b^2+c^2}(a,b,c)$.

concepts: Mid-point of a segment and vector addition in a quadrilateral
questions.question: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral. If $E$ and $F$ are the mid-points of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively and $(\overrightarrow{AB}-\overrightarrow{BC})+(\overrightarrow{AD}-\overrightarrow{DC})=k\,\overrightarrow{FE}$, then $k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write every vector as (head - tail) in position vectors; the sum becomes $2(\vec b+\vec d)-2(\vec a+\vec c)$, i.e. a multiple of $\overrightarrow{EF}$.
solution: Let the position vectors of $A,B,C,D$ be $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$.
Mid-point of $AC$: $E=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}2$; mid-point of $BD$: $F=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec d}2$.
$(\overrightarrow{AB}-\overrightarrow{BC})+(\overrightarrow{AD}-\overrightarrow{DC})=(\vec b-\vec a)-(\vec c-\vec b)+(\vec d-\vec a)-(\vec c-\vec d)$.
$=2\vec b-2\vec a-2\vec c+2\vec d=2(\vec b+\vec d)-2(\vec a+\vec c)$.
useful_results: For any quadrilateral $ABCD$: $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AD}+\overrightarrow{CB}+\overrightarrow{CD}=4\overrightarrow{EF}$, where $E,F$ are the mid-points of $AC,BD$.
$E=F$ (the diagonals bisect each other) iff $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
$\overrightarrow{AB}-\overrightarrow{BC}$ is not a side-chain: rewrite with $-\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{CB}$ before adding.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane, distance of a point from a plane
Quadratic equation with given roots
questions.question: Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the line $\dfrac{x+3}3=\dfrac{y+2}1=\dfrac{1-z}2$ and the plane $x+y+z=2$. If the distance of $P$ from the plane $3x-4y+12z=32$ is $q$, then $q$ and $2q$ are the roots of the equation:
questions.key_idea: Parametrise the line to get $P$, find $q$ with the distance formula, and use sum $3q$ and product $2q^2$ of the roots.
solution: The equation with roots $q$ and $2q$ is $x^2-3qx+2q^2=0$.
useful_results: Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz=d$ is $\dfrac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; here $\sqrt{9+16+144}=13$.
The equation with roots $r,s$ is $x^2-(r+s)x+rs=0$; for roots $q,2q$ it is $x^2-3qx+2q^2=0$.
In the symmetric form $\dfrac{1-z}2$, the $z$-coordinate is $1-2\lambda$ (direction ratio $-2$), not $1+2\lambda$.
Sum $3q=18$ and product $2q^2=72$ are both positive, which rules out options (A), (B) and (C).

concepts: Vector triple product and unit vector perpendicular to a vector
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are non-zero vectors and $\hat n$ is a unit vector perpendicular to $\vec c$ such that $\vec a=\alpha\vec b-\hat n\ (\alpha\neq0)$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=12$, then $|\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Expand $\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)$ by BAC-CAB, use $\vec a\cdot\vec c=12\alpha$ to get $12(\vec a-\alpha\vec b)=-12\hat n$.
solution: $\hat n\cdot\vec c=0$, $|\hat n|=1$, $\vec a=\alpha\vec b-\hat n$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=12$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec c=\alpha\,\vec b\cdot\vec c-\hat n\cdot\vec c=12\alpha-0=12\alpha$.
$\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=(\vec c\cdot\vec b)\vec a-(\vec c\cdot\vec a)\vec b$.
$\vec a-\alpha\vec b=-\hat n$, so $|\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)|=12|\hat n|=12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $\vec a$ first: $\vec a\times\vec b=(\alpha\vec b-\hat n)\times\vec b=-\hat n\times\vec b$.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=\alpha(\vec b\times\vec b)-\hat n\times\vec b=-\hat n\times\vec b$.
$\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=-\vec c\times(\hat n\times\vec b)=-\big[\hat n(\vec c\cdot\vec b)-\vec b(\vec c\cdot\hat n)\big]$.
$\vec c\cdot\vec b=12$ and $\vec c\cdot\hat n=0$, so the vector equals $-12\hat n$.

useful_results: BAC-CAB: $\vec p\times(\vec q\times\vec r)=\vec q(\vec p\cdot\vec r)-\vec r(\vec p\cdot\vec q)$.
If $\vec a=\alpha\vec b+\vec w$ then $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec w\times\vec b$ (the part of $\vec a$ parallel to $\vec b$ drops out).
$\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)$ lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$ and is perpendicular to $\vec c$.

concepts: Direction cosines and equation of a plane normal to a vector
questions.question: A vector $\vec v$ in the first octant is inclined to the $x$-axis at $60^\circ$, to the $y$-axis at $45^\circ$ and to the $z$-axis at an acute angle. If a plane passing through the points $(\sqrt2,-1,1)$ and $(a,b,c)$ is normal to $\vec v$, then:
questions.key_idea: Direction cosines $\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac1{\sqrt2},\tfrac12\right)$ give the normal; the plane is $\vec v\cdot(\vec r-\vec r_0)=0$.
solution: Let $\vec v=l\hat i+m\hat j+n\hat k$ (direction cosines); $l=\cos60^\circ=\dfrac12$ and $m=\cos45^\circ=\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$.
$n=\pm\dfrac12$; $n=-\dfrac12$ is rejected because $\vec v$ is in the first octant, so $n=\dfrac12$.
Direction ratios of the normal can be taken as $1,\sqrt2,1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The given point $(\sqrt2,-1,1)$ lies on the plane, so it must satisfy the correct relation: test the four options with $(a,b,c)=(\sqrt2,-1,1)$.

useful_results: Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; a first-octant vector has all of $l,m,n>0$ (here $n=\tfrac12$).
The plane through $\vec r_0$ normal to $\vec v$ is $\vec v\cdot(\vec r-\vec r_0)=0$; any scalar multiple of $\vec v$ may be used.
If a point is given to lie on the plane, substituting it into candidate answers eliminates options quickly.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points
questions.question: If the four points with position vectors $3\hat i-4\hat j+2\hat k,\ \hat i+2\hat j-\hat k,\ -2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k$ and $5\hat i-2\alpha\hat j+4\hat k$ are coplanar, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Four points are coplanar iff the three vectors from one point to the others have zero scalar triple product.
solution: Take the vectors from the fourth point $D(5,-2\alpha,4)$ to $A(3,-4,2),\ B(1,2,-1),\ C(-2,-1,3)$; coplanarity gives a zero determinant.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's step 'reduced determinant' replaces the first row by $(0,2\alpha-4,-2)$ and changes the first column of the other rows to $-1$ and $6$ without stating an operation that does this (no single row or column operation of the shown determinant gives it). The reduced determinant still evaluates to $17(2\alpha-4)-78=34\alpha-146$, the same as the direct expansion, so the final value is unchanged; the solution is written with a direct expansion instead.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the plane through the first three points via a cross product and require the fourth to lie on it.

useful_results: Four points $A,B,C,D$ are coplanar iff $[\overrightarrow{AB}\ \overrightarrow{AC}\ \overrightarrow{AD}]=0$ (a $3\times3$ determinant of differences).
The plane through three points has normal $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$.
Row/column operations may be used on the determinant, but keep each operation legitimate; compare the unknown coefficient directly.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points and scalar triple product
questions.question: If four distinct points with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are coplanar, then $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ is equal to:
options: $[\vec a\,\vec d\,\vec b]+[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]+[\vec d\,\vec b\,\vec c]$
$[\vec d\,\vec b\,\vec a]+[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec d]+[\vec d\,\vec b\,\vec c]$
$[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]+[\vec b\,\vec d\,\vec a]+[\vec c\,\vec d\,\vec b]$
$[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]+[\vec d\,\vec a\,\vec c]+[\vec d\,\vec b\,\vec a]$
questions.answer: (C) $[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]+[\vec b\,\vec d\,\vec a]+[\vec c\,\vec d\,\vec b]$
questions.key_idea: Coplanar points mean $\vec b-\vec a,\ \vec c-\vec a,\ \vec d-\vec a$ are coplanar; expand the zero triple product and match the options by cyclic order.
solution: The points are coplanar, so $\vec b-\vec a,\ \vec c-\vec a,\ \vec d-\vec a$ are coplanar: $[\vec b-\vec a\ \ \vec c-\vec a\ \ \vec d-\vec a]=0$.
Expanding (terms with a repeated vector vanish): $[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]-[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]-[\vec b\,\vec a\,\vec d]-[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec d]=0$.
$[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$, so $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]-[\vec b\,\vec a\,\vec d]-[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec d]$.
$=[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]+[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec d]+[\vec a\,\vec d\,\vec c]$ (swapping two vectors changes the sign).

Cyclic permutations keep a triple product: $[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]=[\vec c\,\vec d\,\vec b]$, $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec d]=[\vec b\,\vec d\,\vec a]$, $[\vec a\,\vec d\,\vec c]=[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]$.
So $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]+[\vec b\,\vec d\,\vec a]+[\vec c\,\vec d\,\vec b]$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Coplanar points satisfy $\vec d=x\vec a+y\vec b+z\vec c$ with $x+y+z=1$; substitute in each bracket of option (C).
solution: Write $\vec d=x\vec a+y\vec b+z\vec c$ with $x+y+z=1$ (affine combination, since the four points are coplanar and $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are non-collinear).
$[\vec d\,\vec c\,\vec a]=y[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]=y[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$ (the $\vec a,\vec c$ parts vanish).
$[\vec b\,\vec d\,\vec a]=z[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec a]=z[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$ and $[\vec c\,\vec d\,\vec b]=x[\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b]=x[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$.
Sum $=(x+y+z)[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$, confirming (C).

useful_results: Four points are coplanar iff $\vec d=x\vec a+y\vec b+z\vec c$ with $x+y+z=1$, iff $[\vec b-\vec a\ \ \vec c-\vec a\ \ \vec d-\vec a]=0$.
A scalar triple product is unchanged by cyclic permutation and changes sign on swapping two vectors; it is zero if two vectors repeat.
Equivalent symmetric form: $[\vec b\,\vec c\,\vec d]-[\vec a\,\vec c\,\vec d]+[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec d]-[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]=0$ for coplanar points.
